utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Mr. Registrar, could we have the case called, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The case, IT-03-66-PT, the Prosecutor against Fatmir Limaj, Haradin Bala, and Isak Musliu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please, can we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour. Andrew Cayley, Alex Whiting, Colin Black for the Office of the Prosecutor. Our case manager is Hasan Younis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: If it please Your Honour. Karim Khan in the absence of lead counsel, Michael Mansfield, for Fatmir Limaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Gregor Guy-Smith. I am co-counsel for Haradin Bala, in the absence of lead counsel at this time, Mr. Murphy. I thank you for letting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Is there a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe there's a slight difficulty with translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I thank you for the honour of being able to appear in front of you, this being my first appearance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Yes, I know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Michael Topolski with Mr. Steven Powles. We represent Mr. Isak Musliu. And I too share my first appearance in front of Your Honour. It's a pleasure to be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Mr. Powles.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Steven Powles, co-counsel for Isak Musliu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Musliu, please. Could you hear in a languages that understandable for you, that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MUSLIU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Bala, please. Do you understand what is said here in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BALA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Okay. And then Mr. Musliu, please. Can you hear whatever is said here in a language that is for you well known?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MUSLIU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do understand it fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, please sit down. Well, we'll start the last -- probably the last Status Conference with me in this case. I have been informed about what is the situation. It seems that disclosure is proceeding at a good pace so far. You have perhaps some problems still with the translation in Albanian or in German and Albanian in some cases, in some particular case, but I am confident that these difficulties can soon be overcome. On the other side, the disclosure according to Article 68 seems to be nearly completed, if I am not wrong. And in any case, if you have some matters that you'd like to bring about at this moment about this aspect of the disclosure, please, I would ask you to speak up. No problem for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We don't have anything to add --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think we're getting the Albanian translation actually on the English Channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: I try to -- it's okay? Please, could you speak now. I understand that in English. Okay. And what about you, the counsel for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, nothing to raise additional to that that was discussed and agreed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you. It's also the case for all of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. There is the matter of a medical report with regard to Mr. Bala.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Yes. And what is this matter? You said that there's no matter you would like to raise now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to issues concerning the disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to another issue, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Topolski, Mr. Powles?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: On disclosure, nothing. There are two other matters I would like to raise, when convenient to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: We'll arrive to that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: I know that in the case of Mr. Bala, Mr. Murphy is stepping down from his place as counsel for the Defence. Well, I had heard about what are the reasons he has, and besides, well, he's of course permitted to leave the Defence. I am expecting that a new counsel for Mr. Bala could be appointed shortly in time, and -- well, I hope this is not going to disturb the schedule that so far seems to be adopted or nearly adopted for this case. There is another point which could be interesting to talk about with, and that is this Chamber is considering trying to call the attention of the Presidency of the Tribunal to pass the case over to another Court, another Chamber, probably the Chamber number II. Of course, it would depend on the Presidency to take the final decision on the subject, and of course, it may be the case that the President could think of another Chamber. I don't know. That's not for us, this Chamber I, to take the decision, so -- but I mean, the thing is going to be mentioned. And this is interesting because it's related with the possibility that the case could be started on October the 1st - perhaps October the 4th, because the 1st is a Friday, but anyway - at the beginning of October, which seems to be agreeable by everybody in all of the parties in the case. There's another procedural point which seems to be nearly settled or settled, and it is that the Prosecution has got from the Defence acceptance of the date of July the 16th to be -- I mean, to make a reply to their motion in the sense of to the position about the witnesses, above all the witnesses that could be acceptable under the 92 bis Rule which is -- I believe you had become in accordance, both parties, that when the Defence counsels could answer by the 16th of the next month about the propositions made or the position taken by the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor afterwards will place the motion for the witness that there will be, as we used to say, paper witnesses, witnesses that will making their testimonies in the way considered by Article or Rule 92 bis. So the only thing I find that has merits for me to mention is the fact that a motion on behalf of Mr. Bala has been introduced for his being subjected to a new medical observation, so as to get a new report about your situation. We had already decided in favour of this motion, and -- well, the decision of the Court is ready and it's going to be filed either today at the end to have day or, most likely next Monday. So that is what I have to say. But I believe that Mr. Topolski has suggested that he would have some other subject to bring about, and please, I give you the floor. In case some of the other parties have also some points to make, well, they will be given the possibility to do so afterwards. So please go ahead, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very grateful. May I raise two matters, please: The first, very short; the second, I hope not too long. The first is this, it arises out of the meeting that we had yesterday, which I think I can say on behalf of all was conducted constructively and in a most helpful atmosphere. It relates to a matter of some concern to all, and that is suggestions - and I shall put it no higher than that - of the possibility of interference and/or of intimidation of witnesses or potential witnesses. We raised that yesterday, and as a result of a subsequent meeting a protocol was considered to be the best way forward. A draft of that protocol was prepared by Mr. Powles, my co-counsel, overnight. We've distributed it to all parties this afternoon. We hope that it will find favour with Mr. Cayley and his team and will be the way in which all parties will conduct themselves hereafter. I simply place that on the record as something that was a leftover from yesterday of some importance. May I then turn to something else of considerable significance, as far as my lay client is concerned, and I think, if I may be permitted also to say, of the other two defendants. Today for the first time for the entirety of his journey from the Detention Centre to this building my lay client was blindfolded. I say "for the first time." Every other time that he's been there - and I think there's been four or five - that blindfold has been applied, as I understand it, for the first five and the last five minutes of the journey. The difference between all other occasions and today is manifest. I raised this yesterday at the meeting. I say no more about the difference between every other occasion and this afternoon; the fact can speak for itself. I have an application, and my application is that this Court should order, for we submit respectively that the Court has jurisdiction so to do, that my client - and I apprehend my colleagues will join in the application - should not be blindfolded at all, again, from this moment on. May I say this in support of that application four submissions - and they are brief. First of all, as we understand it - and our researchers have been speedy but we hope efficient - these three defendants are treated uniquely to anyone else held in it at the Detention Centre or on trial or about to be held on trial at this Court. Secondly, the search in our submission for a justification for such a step, for which we can find no precedent, would have to be an exceptional circumstance. Those words come from the Rules and are only attributed, as far as we can see, to the question of handcuffs and physical restraints. Nowhere in the Rules - and one is not surprised by this - does one find a provision for blindfolding. Consequently, our second submission is that a compelling reason of the most graphic kind would in our submission have to be placed before you, Your Honour, or any of Your Honour's colleagues evidentially to justify such a step. Thirdly, absent any such compelling reason, this is, in our submission, both inhumane and degrading treatment and it has not escaped our clients' notice that they are, as I have indicated, apparently being singled out for this treatment. The Court has the jurisdiction. I have had sent in to you - I hope you received it - a copy of the current edition of "Archbold International Criminal Court's Practice Procedure & Evidence," and, I hope for your convenience, I flagged up for you the various rules that we respectfully submit apply. I don't know if you had, Your Honour, an opportunity to look; perhaps not. May I take you through it swiftly. The submission I make is simply this: That putting these rules together, there is jurisdiction for you to make the order we seek. May I begin at page 842, where one sees Rule --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Excuse me, you said 600?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: There Your Honour will find Rule 83.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Probably I was misdirected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I hope that should be the first flag. I'm taking them --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm taking them in chronological order through the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: I am in page 842.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour sees Rule 83?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Here I find Rule 82 -- 83, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, 83.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: 83, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: "Instruments of restraint." "Instruments of restraint such as handcuffs shall be used only on the order of the registrar as an precaution against escape during transfer or in order to prevent an accused himself injury, injury to others, or to prevent serious damage to property. Instruments of restraint shall been removed when the accused appears before a Chamber or a judge." So there, in that rule, in simple straightforward terms, is a reflection of the position that it is on the order of the Registrar of this Court as a precaution against escape that restraints can be lawfully applied. One moves on, please, if you would, Your Honour, to page 906. Here we are looking at rules governing detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Rule 2, under the heading "Basic principles": "The United Nations shall retain the ultimate responsibility and liability for all aspects of detention pursuant to these rules. All detainees shall be subject to the sole discretion of the Tribunal at all times they are so detained, even though physically absent from the Detention Unit, until final release or transfer to another institution. Subject to the overriding jurisdiction of the Tribunal, the commanding officer --" I'm told I'm speaking too fast. I'll slow down, and I apologise. "...the commanding officer shall have sole responsibility for all aspects of the day-to-day management of the unit, including security an order, and make all decisions relating thereto except where otherwise provided." We respectfully submit that speaks for itself. "All detainees are subject to the sole jurisdiction of this Tribunal at all times." Your Honour, one moves on, if you would, please, to page 913. And here one deals with Rule -- sees Rule 50, under the heading of "Instructs of restraint and the use of force." "Instruments of restraint such as handcuffs shall only be used in the following exceptional circumstances." -- I'm sorry, have I gone too fast?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: No, no, no, I haven't found it. Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour will see this is where get the word "exceptional circumstances" from in this context. And they are set out there. The first relates to precautions against escape during transfer. May I draw your attention, respectfully, to paragraph B of that rule: "In all incidents involving the use of restraint - and we would argue a blindfold is one such - the commanding officer shall consult the medical officer and report to the registrar who may report the matter to the President." That may have some particular potency in the case of Mr. Bala, but I shall leave that to my learned friend, Mr. Guy-Smith. And finally, if you'd be so kind to go to page 919. Rule 90: "Detainees shall at all times be transported in vehicles with adequate ventilation and light and in such a way as will not subject them to unnecessary physical hardship or indignity." This journey my client took today, as he has taken on four or five previous occasions, has in our submission subjected him to indignity. Your Honour, we only raise this and make this invitation for you to make this order in order that the conduct of this trial shall have as little heat generated in it and around it as possible, for that is in the interest of all. And for a defendant to arrive at a building in the condition that my client, and I believe others, was in today - namely, angry, annoyed, and all that goes with the indignity we say he has been suffering - if "suffering" is too high a word, I apologise for it; "undergoing" - then that cannot be conducive to a trial in due course that is both fair and one in which he can adequately participate, as I know this Court would wish him to be completely free to do. I did ask yesterday that a senior officer be available to answer questions. I am told there is none such here, but nonetheless I make the application that I do. I well recognise that there may be material that is placed before a Court confidentially that relates to matters of security, particularly when prisoners are being transported. I seek not to go into that material, for what I say is this: That if there is a concern that my client should not be able to see where he's going, that can be adequately achieved by putting him in a vehicle with blackened windows, or if that's too expensive, by cutting out some cardboard and sticking it on the window. That would achieve the same result. Your Honour, that is the application we make and the basis and the reasons for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Topolski, for the -- what you are telling me. It's a subject -- please sit down. It's a subject of which I am not very happy, and I had already had the occasion in previous Status Conferences of my thoughts about that. The problem is with all these rules you had kindly read apply to internal situations, and we had to put up also with the rules that are established for the services that give us the possibility of bringing here and back the persons accused. I would say that the situation today seems to have been still more unpleasant than on the previous occasion, and I regret it very much. I have been always interested on what is going on. I know that now the Registrar are still dealing with the Ministry of Justice so as to find a solution for this matter, and the case could be still more pressing, if I may say so, when the case will start to be here in court, because this kind of situation could be repeated mostly every day or surely every day. So I would say that I now will limit myself to call again the attention of the Registrar about the point you have made, in that they had to be introduced in the -- let's say, the talks with the people of the Ministry of Justice. But I'll try. If it doesn't go to a good solution in the near future and I keep still being the Pre-trial Judge in this case, to try to, well, push a little bit the matter so as - not a little bit, as far as would be necessary - with the Ministry of Justice to find a suitable solution, which I am very well aware of the matter. You had also mentioned another question which -- well, I wasn't going to talk with in this conference. And before I go any further, I would like to hear the Prosecution about this subject of the possibility of witnesses being intimidated. And I didn't -- the first I know is that you are not so far sure of any evidence of the existence of the case. But please, could you tell me some more about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As I stated yesterday, there has been from the beginning of this case some evidence that witnesses have been interfered with. There is no evidence to indicate that any of the accused or persons linked to them have directly interfered with any of the witnesses, but there is an environment which is insecure, to put it carefully. As a result of that, Mr. Topolski, as he said, has drafted a protocol for the manner in which the Defence will approach Prosecution witnesses to meet with them. We have to look at this; we've looked at it briefly. I think it meets many of the concerns that both the Defence and the Prosecution. And I would emphasise here, as Mr. Topolski has made clear, he takes this issue as seriously as we do. It's not simply a matter of concern to the Prosecution; it's a matter of concern to both parties. So we will look at this protocol and we will get back to the Defence as soon as we can with any suggested amendments. It's likely that we will probably agree to most of it. More than that at the moment, in terms of this particular issue, we cannot do anything further. If we are receiving information that this is becoming a more serious issue, we will come back to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you very much. You have heard what the representative of the Prosecution has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: I am, of course, well aware what has been said by the Prosecutor. The situation is rather on the whole, let's say, intimidating, and one of the reasons for -- let's try to have the case brought to court, to start the hearing of the case, is that also. So I realise that you are aware and perhaps the other members of the other counsels for the Defence. And of course, in case something more substantial materialises, of course this Tribunal will take care of perhaps the starting proceedings for contempt of court or whatever would be the case. So we know what are your concerns and we keep such in mind. So I wonder if some other matter could be brought about by the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We don't have anything further to add, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: What about you? Yes, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you please, a couple of matters. For the sake of clarify, it's correct to say that this is a further protocol that has been agreed by the three legal teams for the three accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: But in fact, way back in October, we for Fatmir Limaj drafted and filed, in fact, ex parte confidentially with the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: -- various protocols which govern the conduct of the team for Mr. Michael Mansfield is responsible for and they govern the contact with various witnesses. And since that time on any occasion that we have contacted a Prosecution witness or somebody the Prosecution has contacted, we have endeavoured to notify the Prosecution of that. So this is not a new invention; it's a further part of a process, which is self-regulating, which is being put in place by the Defence to make sure that later on allegations, unsupported thus far, of witness intimidation should not be easily bandied about; but if they are raised, they should be raised based on clear and concise evidence. So we have done it for the protection of the trial process, of which we are primarily concerned. Your Honour, the second matter relates to the oral application my learned friend Michael Topolski raised. Perhaps none of us in this room except the three accused can truly appreciate or envisage how traumatic it is to be incarcerated and deprived of one's liberty, particularly when, in the case of my client, he is adamant that he is innocent of the charges with which he is charged. So it is by its very nature a traumatic process. This Court and this Tribunal established to give credence to the highest standards of international human-rights law as well as international humanitarian law, is ever mindful, I know, of abiding by those standards. Your Honour, you did say that the rules cited by my learned friend relate to the period of time when the accused were in the physical custody of the Tribunal. In my submission, that is not the case; and that is why, with the greatest respect, I do re-emphasise and remake the application, and I would ask you to rule upon it: That you do order the Dutch authorities to put in place a system which complies with basic standards of human-rights law. Your Honour is of course aware, apart from all the other rules cited, of Article 29 of the Statute, that states "Shall comply with all orders of the Trial Chamber." And, Your Honour, if you order the Dutch authorities not to impose these draconian measures, it may very well fortify the Registrar in his bid to persuade the Dutch authorities to do that which is right. Your Honour, you will know as a matter of public record that the recent situation in Iraq and relating to the treatment of prisoners, that people were blindfolded. And it's a matter of public record that the British and the Americans no longer do that now. One is aware of the opprobrium that much of the international community raised when one considers Guantanamo Bay. It defies credulity, in my submission, that this Court dealing with the individuals that this Court cited -- should be treated in a manner, as far as blindfolding, which is singly unnecessary. Your Honour, of course the Dutch authorities in consultation with the Registrar have a very real concern to ensure that all accused are not -- do not abscond. But, Your Honour, of course, I do reiterate: It is surprising to say, at least, that all of these accused only these three have been singled out. And when one is looking at the intrusive methods needed to restrain individuals, one has to look, in relation to proportionality, at the least intrusive methods necessary to achieve the aim required. Otherwise, of course, the Dutch could strait-jacket everybody. That's the safest option. And if a very easy option has been put forward simply using a blank -- a prison van with blacked-out windows as is used in the United Kingdom and many other jurisdictions, I do not see why this option cannot be taken up by the Court and cannot be accepted by the Dutch authorities. Your Honour, my concern is this is not a new matter, as you noted; it's been raised before Your Honour some months ago, and our concern was raised at that time. And, in fact, at that time, I mentioned the instructions of my client that he was minded not to come to court at all rather than to come to court in these oppressive circumstances. He told me today that he finds it very difficult to concentrate again after he's brought in in this manner. And so, Your Honour, I do ask you to make an order in accordance with the articles that have been cited, which you are clearly entitled to do. Your Honour, the language of the Rules is clear: "When the Registrar is mandated to look and to give orders regarding the provision of instruments of restraint during transfer," that means transfer from a place to a place. It must include by the very definition of the language of the Rule transfer from the Detention Unit to the premises of the Tribunal. So, Your Honour the plain language of the Rules are there. Similarly; Rule 2 that was cited by my learned friend makes it quite clear - these are the rules governing the detention of persons, page 906 - makes it quite clear that "All detainees shall be subject to the sole jurisdiction of the Tribunal even though they're physically absent from the Detention Unit." Now, Your Honour, the language cannot be any clearer than that. It cannot be any clearer than that. So I do move Your Honour to take up this request made by the three Defence teams that are here today and to make an order under the Rules that are conferred upon you in looking after the integrity of this judicial process in making sure that all accused are equally and impartially, and to direct that the Dutch authorities desist from this action which it has not thought to be necessary in any other case. And Your Honour, I do move that you make a ruling on this submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: I thank you. You have made a very broad and, can I say, passionate by justice feelings of the situation, which I would say, is an acceptable course; but I cannot make my decision just now. I'll take that your oral motion is added to the one made by Mr. Topolski. Please sit down. And what I am going to do is, as you know, that the powers of the Pre-Trial Judge are to organise the preparation of the hearings and the case under the supervision of the whole Chamber. I am going to join my colleagues from the Chamber, and I will -- I had already mentioned to them this case, because it's important, but I will really tell them about what you are asking -- or requiring even. And I will -- I suppose that perhaps Mr. Guy-Smith could join you also for -- on behalf of his client also on the same motion that has been made orally by Mr. Khan. And I will try to devise a solution, a prompt solution for this. I appreciate very much your help and your petition, and I will tell you what I could do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, with regard to not only your invitation but also our inclination, I do join in the remarks, both the logic that has been presented by Mr. Topolski, as well as, as you put it, the emotion that has been presented by Mr. Khan, and would like to add another thought, which is quite specific to Mr. Bala, but I think in some sense crystallises the need for this order, which is as follows: As the Court is well aware, Mr. Bala has suffered from a serious medical condition, has suffered heart attacks both prior to his arrest as well as during his incarceration while detained here. His physical state is, I would put it, in the most gentle of senses, somewhat fragile. He has recently been hospitalised. He has recently undergone an operation. And for him to have to suffer not only the indignity of the transportation plan that has been put in place but also the potential danger that could be visited upon him as a result of the fact that he could at any time have another heart attack, and as I understand it, is constantly in need of nitroglycerin, makes the request here in some senses even more poignant, if no other reason, for the consideration of the individual human dignity as regards Mr. Bala. I'm very troubled -- as a matter of fact, I'm deeply troubled by the fact that these three gentlemen have been singled out and I hope that -- and I understand you are too. And I hope that the Trial Chamber does take this matter quickly and issues an order expeditiously so that these men can be afforded the same rights that others have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I appreciate also your petition. Of course, the solution of the case goes through the problem of the maintenance and respect for the human dignity without a special relationship with the health of the person that is suffering this kind of situation. So I'll repeat what I had promised to do, and I don't know what could be the outcome, but I will take care of that. Now I would refer to the accused. Mr. Limaj, please. Do you have any complaint or any matter that you would like to bring about here about -- or in relation with your health and your possibilities to contact with your lawyers, whenever it's necessary or you feel it's necessary? Please tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED LIMAJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the exception of the matters raised here, I have no other problems specifically. I have had regular contact with lawyers as well as the family, within the parameters of what is allowed to us here. I've had no problem. As regards my health, I feel very well. God willing I hope this continues to be the case. The only thing that I request here: We are not seeking anything other than what the others are afforded. I would request here from people who have obligations to me, towards us, not to prejudice, not to show any prejudices before the matter comes to trial. This Trial Chamber will issue its own verdict on our innocence or not, and that is the question of dignity that that I have been trying to defend here. Somebody is precipitating to try and find us guilty, and I think that neither you nor the Prosecutors' Office or me, we all know what the truth is, but so long as nobody has been found guilty, I request that you, Your Honour, you insist that we be treated fairly and equally. We cannot be of a more dangerous nature than the others, and being singled out is an affront to us, to our dignity, but also to the country I come from, because I'm part of a country which has been victimised and a victim of genocide and the terror exerted upon it. Please, I've got nothing else to say as regards the detention conditions over there. We are happy with everything over there. Everything is fine and excellent. We've got nothing to complain about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. Bala, what is your situation in relation with the communication with your counsel and, of course, if you want to speak about your health in relation with the situation you are having in the Detention Unit and where you are retained.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BALA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding communication with family, the Defence counsel and so on, everything is okay, and also the conditions in the Detention Unit are also fine. Not to repeat myself or repeat what was said here before, I have to reassert here that I do not enjoy good health. I'm in a grave condition, actually. And so I do think that this presents a danger to my health. I do not want to repeat here what Mr. Khan [as interpreted] said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bala. Please sit down. We have already an idea of what are the problems that you are confronted with in relation with your health. And as I had said before, to the latest on next Monday you will get a solution about a new report on your health and what would be the possibilities for your being treated still better that you could be than now. Please, Mr. Musliu, what about you in relation with your possibilities to meet with your counsel? And what about your health? If you have any complaint, please speak up now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MUSLIU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the exception of what the Defence lawyers said here, there's no problem that I can foresee. I enjoy good health. I've got no problems with contacting my lawyers and family. I've got nothing else to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. If nobody wants to raise any other question, I would think we have arrived to the last moment of this Status Conference. As I said before, in case the case is transferred to the other Chamber, it will be my last occasion to contact with you, but I take notice of whatever has been said to me and will try to find a solution for that. Thank you. I adjourn the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: adjourned at 4.32 p.m.
